      <content name="title">Brain <span class="qt2">Tumors</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Brain <span class="qt2">Cancer</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt3">Glioma</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Meningioma</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A brain <span class="qt2">tumor</span> is a growth of abnormal <span class="qt1">cells</span> in the tissues of the brain. Brain <span class="qt2">tumors</span> can be benign, with no <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span>, or malignant, with <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span> that grow quickly.  Some are primary brain <span class="qt2">tumors</span>, which start in the brain. Others are metastatic, and they start somewhere else in the body and move to the brain.</p><p>Brain <span class="qt2">tumors</span> can cause many symptoms. Some of the most common are:</p><ul><li>Headaches, often in the morning </li><li>Nausea and vomiting</li><li>Changes in your ability to talk, hear, or see</li><li>Problems with balance or walking</li><li>Problems with thinking or memory </li><li>Feeling weak or sleepy</li><li>Changes in your mood or behavior</li><li>Seizures</li></ul><p>Doctors diagnose brain <span class="qt2">tumors</span> by doing a neurologic exam and tests including an MRI, CT scan, and biopsy. Treatment options include watchful waiting, surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span> with less harm to normal <span class="qt1">cells</span>. Many people get a combination of treatments.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2">Cancer</span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Childhood Brain <span class="qt2">Tumors</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Brain <span class="qt2">tumors</span> are abnormal growths inside the skull. They are among the most common types of childhood <span class="qt2">cancers</span>. Some are benign <span class="qt2">tumors</span>, which aren't <span class="qt2">cancer</span>. They can still be serious. Malignant <span class="qt2">tumors</span> are cancerous.</p><p>Childhood brain and spinal cord <span class="qt2">tumors</span> can cause headaches and other symptoms. However, other conditions can also cause the same symptoms. Check with a doctor if your child has any of the following problems:</p><ul><li>Morning headache or headache that goes away after vomiting</li><li>Frequent nausea and vomiting</li><li>Vision, hearing, and speech problems</li><li>Loss of balance or trouble walking</li><li>Unusual sleepiness</li><li>Personality changes</li><li>Seizures</li><li>Increased head size in infants</li></ul><p>The symptoms are not the same in every child.</p><p>Doctors use physical and neurological exams, lab tests, and imaging to diagnose brain <span class="qt2">tumors</span>. Most childhood brain <span class="qt2">tumors</span> are diagnosed and removed in surgery.</p><p>Treatment for children is sometimes different than for an adult. Long-term side effects are an important issue. The options also depend on the type of <span class="qt2">tumor</span> and where it is. Removal of the <span class="qt2">tumor</span> is often possible. If not, radiation, chemotherapy, or both may be used.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2">Cancer</span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/neurofibromatosis.html">
      <content name="title">Neurofibromatosis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">von Recklinghausen's Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Recklinghausen's disease</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Neurofibromatosis is a genetic disorder of the nervous system. It mainly affects how nerve <span class="qt1">cells</span> form and grow. It causes <span class="qt2">tumors</span> to grow on nerves.  You can get neurofibromatosis from your parents, or it can happen because of a mutation (change) in your genes.  Once you have it, you can pass it along to your children. Usually the <span class="qt2">tumors</span> are benign, but sometimes they can become cancerous.</p><p>There are three types of neurofibromatosis:</p><ul><li>Type 1 (NF1) causes skin changes and deformed bones. It usually starts in childhood.  Sometimes the symptoms are present at birth.</li><li>Type 2 (NF2) causes hearing loss, ringing in the ears, and poor balance. Symptoms often start in the teen years.</li><li>Schwannomatosis causes intense pain. It is the rarest type.</li></ul><p>Doctors diagnose the different types based on the symptoms. Genetic testing is also used to diagnose NF1 and NF2. There is no cure. Treatment can help control symptoms. Depending on the type of disease and how serious it is, treatment may include surgery to remove <span class="qt2">tumors</span>, radiation therapy, and medicines.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/opticnervedisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Optic Nerve Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The optic nerve is a bundle of more than 1 million nerve fibers that carry visual messages. You have one connecting the back of each eye (your retina) to your brain. Damage to an optic nerve can cause vision loss. The type of vision loss and how severe it is depends on where the damage occurs. It may affect one or both eyes.</p><p>There are many different types of optic nerve disorders, including:</p><ul><li>Glaucoma is a group of diseases that are the leading cause of blindness in the United States. Glaucoma usually happens when the fluid pressure inside the eyes slowly rises and damages the optic nerve.</li><li>Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve. Causes include infections and immune-related illnesses such as multiple sclerosis. Sometimes the cause is unknown.</li><li>Optic nerve atrophy is damage to the optic nerve. Causes include poor blood flow to the eye, disease, trauma, or exposure to toxic substances.</li><li>Optic nerve head drusen are pockets of protein and calcium salts that build up in the optic nerve over time</li></ul><p>Contact your health care provider if you are having vision problems. Tests for optic nerve disorders may include eye exams, ophthalmoscopy (an examination of the back of your eye), and imaging tests. Treatment depends on which disorder that you have. With some optic nerve disorders, you may get your vision back. With others, there is no treatment, or treatment may only prevent further vision loss.</p></content>
